title: Quiz: Birth-Death Process — Linear Growth and Extinction

questions.text: In the linear birth-death process, the total event rate when the population is n is:
options: n(λ + μ) (both births and deaths scale with n)
questions.explanation: Total rate = birth rate + death rate = nλ + nμ = n(λ+μ). Both rates are proportional to n because each individual independently gives birth at rate λ and dies at rate μ. In the Gillespie algorithm, the waiting time until the next event (birth or death) is Exp(n(λ+μ)).

questions.text: For the linear birth-death process with λ > μ, the extinction probability from a single initial individual is μ/λ (not 0 and not 1).
questions.explanation: When λ > μ (supercritical, ρ = μ/λ < 1), the extinction probability is exactly ρ = μ/λ ∈ (0,1). The process can grow forever with probability 1-ρ = (λ-μ)/λ, or go extinct by chance with probability ρ. Even in a growing population, early stochastic fluctuations can wipe out the lineage.

questions.text: An epidemic model has R0 = λ/μ = 1.8 (birth rate exceeds death rate). What is the probability that an epidemic starting from 1 infectious case goes extinct?
options: 0 — it always becomes a major epidemic since R0 > 1
questions.explanation: The extinction probability is ρ = μ/λ = 1/R0 = 1/1.8 ≈ 0.556. So even with R0=1.8, there's a 55.6% chance the epidemic dies out spontaneously from a single introduction. A 'major epidemic' only occurs with probability 1-1/R0 ≈ 44.4%.

questions.text: If 3 independently introduced cases each have extinction probability q* = 0.6, what is the probability that ALL three lineages go extinct?
questions.explanation: Each of the 3 lineages independently goes extinct with probability q*=0.6. For all three to go extinct, we need the intersection of three independent events, each with probability 0.6. P(all three extinct) = 0.6 × 0.6 × 0.6 = 0.6^3 = 0.216.

questions.text: At the critical point ρ=1 (λ=μ), what happens to E[N(t)] and Var[N(t)]?
options: Both E and Var are constant for all t
E[N(t)]=1 (constant) but Var[N(t)]=2λt (grows linearly with t)
E[N(t)] grows exponentially and Var[N(t)] is bounded
Both E and Var grow exponentially
questions.explanation: When λ=μ (critical), E[N(t)] = e^{(λ-μ)t} = e^0 = 1 for all t — the expected population stays at its initial value. However, Var[N(t)] = 2λt → ∞. The process is on average unchanged, but individual trajectories become wildly variable — some explode, most go extinct. This is the critical branching phenomenon.

questions.text: The PGF equation ∂G/∂t = (λs-μ)(s-1) ∂G/∂s is a partial differential equation (PDE) because G depends on both s and t.
questions.explanation: G(s,t) = Σ P_n(t) s^n is a function of two variables: the dummy variable s ∈ [0,1] and time t ≥ 0. The equation involves partial derivatives with respect to both t (∂G/∂t) and s (∂G/∂s), making it a PDE. It is first-order in both variables and is solved using the method of characteristics.
